name: SilverLining (charityevals)
summary: SilverLining (Washington, DC) funds and coordinates research on solar radiation modification (cooling the planet by reflecting a little sunlight) and presses governments to research and govern it; this model values that work by the research it added in 2019-2024: its own grants and science, other funders' money it directed, and the US federal research line (NOAA's Earth's Radiation Budget, about $8M a year since 2020) its policy work helped start, against its spending over those years ($6.5M in 2024). A dollar of the field's research is worth a share of the heat deaths a use of cooling would avert, put into tonnes of CO₂ by how much a tonne warms: a 30% chance of a use this century, 0.6°C for 50 years, research adding a tenth of its benefit by improving the decision, over all the field's funding until then. At the defaults a dollar given averts the heat deaths of about 0.7 tonnes of CO₂, about 0.085 years of healthy life per $1,000; it is more than ten times its peers because cooling acts on the warming itself, so the decision research informs weighs hundreds of billions of tonnes, and the field informing it is small (about $44M a year). The result is mostly uncertainty, resting on judgments no study settles (how much research improves that decision, whether cooling is used at all), and every branch is discounted for missing data.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: SilverLining

rows.label: Cooling if solar radiation modification is used, averaged over its years
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.6°C (0.2 to 1.2): the size of a use the research informs. Anchor: the most studied design, ARISE-SAI (Richter et al. 2022; SilverLining's grants and its chief scientist took part), starts injections in 2035 and holds warming at 1.5°C above pre-industrial under the intermediate scenario SSP2-4.5, which the IPCC puts at 2.0°C in 2041-2060 and 2.7°C in 2081-2100 (Table SPM.1): a cooling of about 0.5°C at mid-century rising to 1.2°C by its end. Lower if it is used only to shave a peak, or under lower emissions.

source.title: Richter et al. (2022), Assessing Responses and Impacts of Solar climate intervention on the Earth system with stratospheric aerosol injection (ARISE-SAI), Geoscientific Model Development 15, 8221
source.quote: keep global mean surface air temperature near 1.5 °C above the pre-industrial value

rows.label: Years solar radiation modification is used, if used
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 50 years (20 to 100): holding back warming while emissions fall and carbon is removed takes decades (ARISE's design runs to 2069 and its successors beyond); a short use ends early by choice or by a halt.

rows.label: Chance solar radiation modification is used at a climate-relevant scale this century
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 30% (10% to 60%): 66% of 120 IPCC-contributing researchers who answered a 2025 survey expect a large-scale deployment attempt this century; an attempt is not a sustained use of the size above, and respondents chose to answer, so the best guess is about half of it. Not marked a single event: like the catastrophe chances by 2100 (facts: catastrophe), it is a forecast about the world every dollar of the field faces, not a bet this charity makes, and better research also has value in the worlds where it is not used (a harmful use avoided, in decision_value_share).

source.title: SRM360 (30 October 2025), Scientists expect an SRM deployment attempt this century (New Scientist survey)
source.quote: a similar proportion expect a large-scale deployment attempt this century

rows.label: Share of the cooling's benefit the field's research adds through better decisions
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 10% (2% to 30%): research does not cool the planet; it changes whether, when and how cooling is used. Its value is the difference between the decisions made with it and without it: a well-designed use (injection sites and amounts that limit regional harms such as shifted monsoons, an end that avoids a sudden rebound) instead of a crude one, and a harmful use avoided. We count that as a share of the gross benefit of the use. No study estimates it; the anchor is that without research a use would still be possible (it is cheap) but blind, and that survey respondents name unknown consequences as the main risk (80%, SRM360's summary of the 2025 survey).

rows.label: Years over which a tonne's heat deaths are counted
rows.explainer: From the emission year to the end of Rethink Priorities' count (2020-2300), the years over which the shared heat-death rate spreads a tonne's warming.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂ whose heat deaths the cooling would avert, if used
rows.explainer: Cooling × years ÷ (a tonne's warming × the years its heat deaths are counted): a cooling of 0.6°C for 50 years spares the heat deaths of about 240 billion tonnes, about six years of the world's emissions. It puts cooling into the site's tonnes so the shared conversion values it (normalization.md 2.5); only heat deaths, since cooling doesn't remove the air pollution of fuel.

rows.label: Funding for all solar radiation modification work, per year, 2021-2025
rows.explainer: Everyone's spending on the field each year (research 50%, awareness and advocacy 21%, the rest outdoor tests, governance and commercial work), philanthropic, government and commercial, SilverLining's own funders included. The range is ours: the tracker counts only transactions it knows of, and its own totals differ slightly between figures.

source.title: SRM360 (September 2026), Who funds work on solar geoengineering? (2026 funding tracker)
source.quote: only about $44 million per year in overall funding for SRM between 2021 and 2025

rows.label: Average yearly funding until a decision, as a multiple of 2021-2025's
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 2× (1× to 4×): funding grew more than tenfold in a decade (SRM360), and the UK's ARIA alone committed about $77M over several years; it may keep growing as warming passes 1.5°C, or stall as governments pull back (SRM360 notes other governments falling back).

rows.label: Years of the field's work that inform the decision
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 20 years (10 to 35): research from about 2020 until a decision to use it or not, which the 2025 survey's respondents and ARISE's 2035 start place in the 2030s to 2050s.

rows.label: All funding for the field until a decision
Tonnes a typical dollar of the field's work is worth
rows.explainer: The chance of use × the tonnes its heat deaths equal × the share research adds, over all the field's funding until the decision: an average dollar of the field. SilverLining's dollars enter below at this value, with their own adjustments. At the defaults about 4 tonnes a dollar (25 cents a tonne) before any adjustment, against $0.50-3.50 a tonne for the climate funds' best picks (facts: climate, top_climate_fund_usd_per_tco2e): cheaper because cooling would offset the warming of hundreds of billions of tonnes at once, and the field whose research shapes that decision spends about $44M a year. This is why the model is far above the climate median (its peers' tonnes are each a policy's emissions cut); after its adjustments it is near the climate funds' best picks.

rows.label: Probability the outcome happens because of this work
rows.explainer: 1: the grants were made, the money directed and the federal line won in the period; the chances (of use, of research mattering) are in the value of a field dollar above.

rows.label: Years the federal research line counts
rows.explainer: The site's one answer for a won reform (docs/normalization.md 2.9): the programme's yearly money counts for the years it came earlier than it would have.

rows.label: Years from the work until the heat deaths it averts start to count
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0 (0 to 15): the deaths come while cooling is used (about 2040 to 2090, centred some 40 years from now); the shared conversion already counts a tonne's heat deaths 60 years after it is avoided, a little later than that, so no further wait is added (which counts these deaths slightly later than they come). The high end is a use that starts late in the century.

rows.label: Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate; the unit's conversion then discounts the heat deaths, so nothing is discounted twice.

rows.label: Years the federal line counts, discounted
Years the federal line counts, discounted, after the wait
Its other policy results, as a share of the federal line's value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 30% (5% to 100%): the White House's congressionally mandated research plan (2023), which it says its advocacy supported; research it funded that informed the UN ozone assessment (2022) and UN Environment Programme's One Atmosphere report (2023); and its engagement of scientists and officials in Africa, the Global South and the Arctic. They shape the decisions research informs, as the federal line does, but no money or rule follows from them.

Directed money: tonnes of the research it steered, before adjustments
Policy branch: tonnes of the federal research line and its other policy results, before adjustments
All branches, before adjustments
Trust in the chain from research dollars to heat deaths
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 1): cooling is not the reverse of a tonne: it cools the tropics more than the poles and changes rainfall, so heat deaths in the hot places where most of them happen may fall a little less than a tonne-for-tonne reckoning says; the share research adds is a guess with no study behind it. As for Project Drawdown's research (0.7).

rows.label: Research: share that wouldn't have been funded anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 80% (50% to 95%): in 2020-2022 its research initiative was one of few funders of such modelling; others (philanthropy, the UK's ARIA from 2024) would have funded some of the same work later.

rows.label: Research: its grants' share of the resources behind the work they funded
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 70% (40% to 100%): the host institutions' own staff, computing (NCAR's supercomputers for ARISE) and overheads, which the funding tracker doesn't count, add to its money.

rows.label: Research: share of credit used
rows.explainer: Its share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Directed money: share that wouldn't have gone to equally useful research anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 40% (15% to 70%): funders who put money into the work it coordinated were already interested in the field; some of the money would have gone to similar research without it.

rows.label: Directed money: its share of the work behind the funders' choices
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 60% (30% to 90%): the funders' own staff and the researchers who pitched the projects share the credit for where the money went.

rows.label: Directed money: share of credit used
rows.explainer: Its share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Federal line: share that is a gain over what the money would otherwise have done
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 70% (30% to 95%): the line was set aside inside NOAA's research budget, so part of it displaced other atmospheric research of some value; when it came earlier than it would have is in the years counted, not here (one question each).

rows.label: Federal line: SilverLining and its lobbying arm's share of the work behind it
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 30% (10% to 60%): it was one of only two organisations to disclose lobbying on solar geoengineering in the decade to 2023 (the other Carnegie Mellon University, in 2013: E&E News, 2 March 2023, 'Blocking sun rays finds support in the Senate'), and its director consulted on the bill behind the line (MIT Technology Review); the decision was Congress's, with NOAA's own scientists, members such as Rep. McNerney and the National Academies' 2021 call for a federal programme behind it.

rows.label: Side effect: atmospheric science that serves other uses, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, +10% (+2% to +30%): measurements and models of aerosols and clouds it funded serve weather and climate science beyond cooling: the Hunga eruption balloon campaign, ship-plume measurements relevant to the warming from the 2020 cut in shipping's sulphur, and the stratospheric observations of the federal line.

rows.label: Side effect: less effort to cut emissions because cooling looks possible, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, -3% (-15% to +2%): research that makes cooling look feasible could weaken the push to cut emissions; survey experiments find the effect small, and some find the opposite (people told of geoengineering support cuts more), so the range runs through zero.

rows.label: Side effect: a hasty or ungoverned use made likelier, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, -8% (-30% to -1%): research and advocacy that make cooling familiar can make an early use by one country or a company likelier (a start-up released sulphur balloons in 2022; a venture-funded firm now develops a proprietary particle), with the harms research is meant to prevent. Small beside the value, since SilverLining backs open research and government oversight, and such actors don't depend on it.

rows.label: Share of the tonnes from burning less fuel
rows.explainer: 0: cooling averts heat deaths only; it removes no fuel smoke (the air pollution of the sulphate particles themselves, if used, is a harm of the use inside decision_value_share).

rows.label: Smoke per tonne of the fuel avoided, relative to the average
rows.explainer: 0: no fuel is avoided (fuel_share is 0).

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Read by the tco2e unit's conversion (docs/normalization.md 2.5).
